newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers vow to continue blockade until Xmas.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers vow to continue blockade until Xmas.

text.p: Defiant Greek farmers erected more road blockades on Tuesday, causing transport chaos for a sixth day, and vowed to continue their action over Christmas to press demands for better prices and cheaper fuel.

"I am putting up the Christmas tree on the tractor because I don't expect to be home by the holidays. We'll stay here for as long as it takes and the government must realise this," Antonis Kalogirou, a farmer on a roadblock outside the central town of Larissa, told reporters.

The week-long blockade has caused chaos at more than 40 spots on the national road network with the farmers brushing off government pleas to end the protest and warnings of inflicting heavy damage on the economy.
"I will stay here because I have nothing to lose. In the next three months the bank will confiscate my house because I can't pay back my loan," said cotton grower Yannis Angelakis.

The protest, backed by a motley army of some 10,000 tractors, is pressing demands for lower fuel prices, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on equipment, higher farm subsides and the rescheduling of some $1.3 billion in debts with state banks.
The queues of trapped international and domestic lorries grew.
"We've been here for three days with no food, no water, no toilets," an international driver told reporters at the western port of Patras.
He was carrying a cargo from Germany to a NATO base on the island of Crete. He had crossed from Italy before being trapped by the farmers.
Hundreds of trucks could be seen stretching along highways while others tried to inch their way along narrow country lanes to skirt the barricades.
Bonfires of tyres lit up the night. Despite bitter cold and rain, farmers have set up sprawling motorway camps with chairs, tables and plastic tent shelters.
A similar protest in 1995 lasted 10 days, sent food prices soaring and cost the economy tens of millions of dollars but the farmers seemed in a festive mood and unconcerned about economic damage.
"We're farmers. We work the fields. That's our job. Farmers can't go to Brussels to protest for their rights. That's the goverment's job," Dimitris Paskos told Reuters Television.
The government has said its hands are tied by European Union regulations which ban member states from subsidising produce prices.
Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis said he would announce his position on the protests after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday.

"Intransigence does not benefit the farmers' problems or the country. The government is not prepared to negotiate the course of the country. Everyone must understand that the situation must not and cannot continue," said government spokesman Yannis Nikolaou.
Asked if police would force open the roads, Nikolaou said: "We have not reached the point to be discussing such an option."
